edge.title: The first twenty minutes after your phone goes
edge.setup: Phone gone — snatched at a signal, lifted on a bus, left in an auto. The handset is the small loss. What's sitting on it: UPI apps, bank OTPs arriving by SMS, email that can reset every password you own, photos of documents. On a Deepavali weekend, bus stands, railway stations and signals are at their most crowded.
edge.tell: The sequence is SIM, then banking, then handset — in that order, and the order is the whole thing.
move: Block the SIM first, from any phone. While it's live, every OTP you own is being delivered to the thief.
From a laptop: sign out of all sessions on Google/Apple, then freeze UPI and net banking.
Block the handset itself on ceir.gov.in using the IMEI — it bricks the device across all networks in India. File the FIR; you'll need it.
Keep your IMEI somewhere that isn't your phone. Today.
edge.why: People instinctively chase the hardware and lose the accounts. The thief's value is almost never resale — it's the twenty-minute window where your SMS inbox is in their hand. Speed on the SIM beats everything else combined.
edge.variants: Same shape: a lost wallet (cards before cash), a compromised email (sessions before password), a stolen laptop (remote wipe before FIR).

lens.name: Second-order effects
lens.one_line: The first consequence of a change is usually obvious and usually not the one that matters.
lens.detail: First order: a metro line opens, your commute drops 40 minutes. Second order: everyone else's does too, so rents near the stations rise, which prices out the people the line was meant to serve, which changes who rides it. Most policy arguments are conducted entirely in first-order terms, which is why they keep surprising everyone.
elsewhere: A subsidy lowers a price, so demand rises, so the queue becomes the real cost.
A company bans a tool, so work routes through an unmonitored one.
Rent control holds rents, so landlords stop maintaining and supply shrinks.
lens.test: Ask 'and then what?' three times. The answer that surprises you is where the real story is.
lens.today: From 6 November, buses and goods vehicles are barred from Ballari Road for 18 months while the BDA builds an elevated corridor, per The Times of India and The Economic Times. The first-order effect is a smoother road once it is done; the second-order effects arrive sooner, as heavy traffic shifts to neighbouring roads and timings, which then carry more than they were built for. Plan around where the diverted traffic goes, not just around the closure itself.

moved.what: From 6 November, KSRTC buses and goods vehicles are banned on Ballari Road for 18 months while the BDA builds an elevated corridor, with traffic diversions announced (Times of India, Economic Times).
moved.so_what: If your route to the airport or north Bengaluru uses Ballari Road, check the traffic police diversion advisory before you leave and add buffer time. Expect the roads that absorb the diversion to slow too.

moved.what: This weekend's Deepavali getaway is expected to bring a massive vehicle outflow from Bengaluru (Times of India). Special trains run between Bengaluru, Mangaluru and Goa on 7 and 8 November, and Bengaluru–Belagavi specials have also been announced.
moved.so_what: If you are travelling out, leave before the afternoon or after the late-evening peak, or book one of the special trains instead of driving. If you are staying in town, avoid the highway-bound roads on Friday evening and Saturday morning.

moved.what: BMTC bus fares and passes have gone up, with passes reported 25% higher; Deccan Herald says commuters now pay more than on Namma Metro for slower journeys, and a bus riders' group has demanded a rollback.
moved.so_what: Recompute your monthly commute cost this week: pass versus daily fares versus Metro for your own route. For some routes the Metro may now be cheaper and faster.

moved.what: The Times of India reports that Karnataka voter lists show duplicates and errors after the special intensive revision.
moved.so_what: Search for your name and details on the electoral roll now. A wrong or duplicated entry is easier to fix before an election than on polling day.

moved.what: Reuters reports tankers were hit in the Strait of Hormuz as Iran keeps up pressure after the US vote.
moved.so_what: This is a watch item, not an alert. Hormuz disruption is the route by which crude, and eventually petrol, diesel and LPG prices, can move, so do not panic-buy fuel but expect the next few weeks of price news to matter.

carry_over.prompt: A video of a public figure announces a government-backed trading platform, and a small test withdrawal actually reaches your account. What is the one thing to check?
carry_over.answer: A guaranteed return. Nothing legitimate guarantees one — the video is irrelevant.
